Kohler, who coordinated defense system development for America's European allies during the Obama administration, described the current setup as "frozen in time because our overall military budget was so constrained."
"You can fix the sensors but there is no longer the capability, basically due to the missile penetration radar, to pick up missiles coming in... unless you expose large quantities of interceptors that might not be needed to begin with," Kohler said during a recent panel discussion on nuclear defense policy at the Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University.
"You don't know if part of the incoming ballistic missile attack was made of cruise missiles, guided by North Korean missile technology right in your face. So your interceptor would not have any way of detecting the incoming threat and responding to it," he added.
One especially worrying advanced Russian cruise missile has a range that vastly surpasses what the Pentagon would require to defend the continental United States, but it would predominantly cover its overseas territories like Europe.

"This may be a challenge that just is either unsolvable or causes us to have to resort to possible use of the full array of our forces," said Michael O'Hanlon, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank.
Meanwhile, Boeing, which leads America's missile-defense contractors, announced in February a contract with the Pentagon for delivering components of an advanced missile interceptor to be constructed in Maryland.
One such interceptor will be included in a new missile-defense system costing nearly $1 billion and due to be completed in Romania sometime before the end of the year, according to the MDA.
Another project, called Aegis Ashore, provides five additional "defense as needed" strategic locations, to protect against so-called "limited provocative strikes using theatre ballistic missiles from regional powers," according to MDA plans.
At another plant in Romania, one such system is being developed.
